text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Four leading Danish pension funds are to embark on proceedings against Den Danske Bank over the sale of shares in now defunct Hafnia insurance in 1992. They are to sue the bank, French Paribas and a Danish broker firm for some 80 million crowns in compensation, claiming that the banks were negligent in selling its customers shares in Hafnia shortly before it went bankrupt.

--Top economists including a former "wiseman" welcome rumours that the Social Democrat-led government is working on a 10 billion crown emergency fiscal package designed to curb domestic private consumption and head off any overheating of Denmark's economy.

--Trade minister Jan Troejborg is not to intervene against BG Bank for practising ethical banking by cancelling accounts of politically unacceptable clients such as Denmark's Anti-Immigration Society, claiming that organisations who feel discriminated against can take legal action against the bank.
-- Danish sugar producer Danisco, which also has a monopoly of beet production in Sweden is fighting a losing battle for a refund of 400 million crowns in excessive tax from the Swedish state.
--Denmark's furniture industry is in trouble, finding it hard to earn sufficient profits, with home as well as office furnishing hard hit by falling sales.

--Leading Danish bedclothes, duvet, eiderdown and bedlinen company Jysk Sengetoejslager is enjoying a period of major expansion, opening eight new outlets in Moscow and franchise shops in the Faroe Islands, Greenland, Iceland and Canada.

--A survey of Danish export expectations shows sharply declining optimism about prospects for the timber, furniture and wholesale industries with the chemical, textile and clothing sectors only slightly more pessimistic than before.

--Danish banks suffer from excessive liquidity and could easily loan 300 million crowns to customers without feeling it or hurting their solidity but Danes are saving as rarely before and not interested in taking out loans, a survey shows.
